title: Portfolio Update (GTX, MSB, FRMO, TPL)
summary:
We purchased Garrett Motion, ticker symbol GTX, in 2020, when it was going through bankruptcy
and it's the largest special situation in our portfolios. Earlier this month, my co-host and I traveled to New York City and attended FRMO's annual
shareholder meeting, highlights from the trip included iconic sightseeing, lunch
with two friends from Horizon It continues to confound us how few investors appreciate the unique wisdom of Maurice Stahl
and ignore what he and his team are building at Horizon Kinetics and FRMO.

transcript:
Welcome to episode 133 of Special Situation Investing.
It's been three months since our last portfolio update.
We use these pieces to summarize updates from quarterly reports and earnings calls of
companies in our portfolios and occasional honorable mentions from our watchlist.
The goal is to record highlights in a succinct format, capturing our thoughts, for future
reflection.
We hope you find these updates valuable.
Bring it off with Garrett Motion.
We purchased Garrett Motion, ticker symbol GTX, in 2020, when it was going through bankruptcy
and it's the largest special situation in our portfolios.
While we don't intend to hold Garrett long-term, it does have characteristics we like to
see in quality companies, namely, plenty of free cash flow and shareholder friendly management.
Consider the following quote from the company's conference call, quote.
This quarter we repurchased $65 million of common stock, bringing our total repurchases
in the first half of 2024 to $174 million.
Since the successful conversion of our preferred stock last year, we have reduced our debt
by $394 million.
At the same time, we have repurchased $958 million in stock, or 34% of shares outstanding.
End quote.
Annualizing Garrett's second quarter free cash flow of $62 million, the company trades
at a yield of 14% on a $1.8 billion market cap.
Management is vocal about its intention to continue returning cash to shareholders through
debt repayment and sharey purchases.
Quote.
We will continue to use our strong cash generation to acquire more shares in the second half.
All the actions taken are driven towards making Garrett a highly attractive investment with
potential for significant additional upside.
End quote.
Out of making Garrett highly attractive, in our opinion, includes obtaining a debt rating
of at least BB, or triple B, excuse me.
The company's progress in that direction over the last quarter was mentioned by the CFO.
Quote.
These actions, paying down and refinancing debt, that the CEO mentioned are expected to generate
annual interest savings of approximately $15 million.
Importantly, these changes contributed to upgrades of our credit ratings of our secured
debt from both S&P and Moody's to BB Plus and BA1 respectively.
End quote.
Check in the chart below of S&P and Moody ratings.
One can see that Garrett at BB Plus and BA1 is only one level below investment grade.
We are looking forward to watching what happens when this high cash flowing company becomes
available to more institutional investors.
Misabi Trust.
In a press release on September 10, Misabi Trust, ticker symbol MSB, announced the end of
its litigation against Cleveland Cliffs.
The ruling wasn't favor of the trust, concluding that the trust had been underpaid to the tune
of approximately $60 million.
Here are the details from the press release.
Quote.
The trust received the final award on September 6, 2024, which unanimously awarded the trust
damages in the amount of approximately $60 million for underpaid royalties in 2020,
2021, and the first four months of 2022, plus pre-award interest in the amount of approximately
$11 million calculated at the rate of 10% simple interest per annum from the date of the initial
demand through September 1, 2024, and continuing to accrue until paid.
Pursuant to the award, Cliffs and North Shore must pay the trust the amount specified in
the award by no later than October 6, 2024.
End quote.
At the time of the announcement, $71 million was about 30% of the company's market cap.
The following day, the stock jumped more than 20% and has drifted upward since.
But even after this rise, the market is not fully pricing in what this announcement means
for Misabi.
Consider that $71 million is worth $5.42 per unit, with 13.1 million units for Misabi.
Since Misabi is a trust and simply passes all of its earnings to its unit holders, we
expect this large payout to be distributed within the next few months.
Hypothetically, if one bought the stock at its current price of $21.57 and subtracted
out the upcoming distribution, it's as if one is paying only $16.15 for the stock.
Misabi's current dividend is $0.30, yielding about 6%.
While we haven't checked this number ourselves, Maurice Stahl recently said, Misabi's legal
fields, legal fees for this lawsuit, were about 20 cents per unit per quarter.
If those fees are no longer required, the quarterly dividend could increase to approximately 50
cents.
That would be a 9.2% yield on the current price and a 12.4% yield on a cost basis after
subtracting out the one-time distribution.
While we're not actively allocating to Misabi at this time, let's just say we're happy
we kept the dividend reinvest going.
FRMO Corp.
Earlier this month, my co-host and I traveled to New York City and attended FRMO's annual
shareholder meeting, highlights from the trip included iconic sightseeing, lunch
with two friends from Horizon Kinetics, and meeting Maurice Stahl.
In contrast, the shareholder meetings of Berkshire Hathaway and recently NVIDIA, this meeting
was intimate with fewer than two dozen attendees.
It continues to confound us how few investors appreciate the unique wisdom of Maurice Stahl
and ignore what he and his team are building at Horizon Kinetics and FRMO.
An audio, soon to be transcript, of Stahl's talk at the meeting is posted on FRMO's
website.
Here's my main learning point.
Texas is unique in regard to its water regulations.
Stahl said, quote, Texas in the world of water is probably unique in the world.
The reason it's unique in the world is, Texas has what's called the rule of capture.
Meaning, if the water runs through your property, you can do, within reason, more or
less, whatever you want with the water.
Everywhere else in the world, you really can't do that.
There's also the L Capitan Reef, this huge underground river that basically runs underneath
the Delaware basin.
So it's a unique geological structure as well.
If you own the land, you can't do that in Canada.
You can't even do that in most places in the United States.
You could never provide the amount of water that's needed.
So that's why if you look at the other hydrocarbon basins in the United States, the
eagle forward, the Haynesville, the Nairobiara, etc., well, you'll find us.
The limiting factor is water.
Can't get the water.
So if you can't get the water, you can't do the fracking.
If you can't get the water, you can't do the data centers.
You might say California is the American Center for Technology.
So you'd wonder why we wouldn't build a lot of data centers there.
Well, there are a lot of data centers there, but the modern data centers are going to
need a lot of water in what is California short of, water.
So obviously, there's a limit to how many data centers you can build in the state of California.
So data centers have to go where the water is, fortunately or unfortunately, depending on
your point of view.
End quote.
Therefore, in addition to the cheap energy, abundant-produced water, and unregulated energy grid, and vast
open spaces, our two Permian Basin land companies, Landbridge and Texas Pacific, also have favorable
regulations supporting their water investments.
The number of tailwinds behind these two companies just keeps growing.
Regarding Landbridge specifically, yours truly asked, stall, what regulations or economic
incentives caused produced water to flow out of New Mexico across Landbridge property
in Texas, and then back into New Mexico.
Here's stall's reply, quote, Landbridge talks about the investment opportunity of water
that's coming from or going to New Mexico.
What is the regulation in New Mexico?
So unlike Texas, New Mexico does not allow you to dispose of water in the ground.
So this refers to produced water.
There's two kinds of water.
There's sourced water and produced water.
Sourced water is what you pump into the well to frack.
Fresh water is the water that comes out of the well, in primordial times, in addition
to carbon-based life forms that basically decayed inside sandstone, water got in there as well.
When you fracture the sandstone, the water is released and comes to the surface as well.
It's not a big problem, separating oil from water, but you now can't take that water
and pump it back into the ground.
The water must be transported to Texas.
Landbridge doesn't transport that water, a sister company of Landbridge known as Waterbridge,
which is owned by the same people, 5-point energy, they do the water transport.
And Landbridge gets a tariff from that and could further benefit from that because you
could, in theory, dispose of that water on Landbridge property.
So what's the other Landbridge opportunity?
You need sourced water.
Texas has a lot more water than New Mexico.
And there's also restrictions on using sourced water in New Mexico.
New Mexico is much stricter.
By the way, it's not just state, it's also federal.
A lot of the exploration occurs on federal lands.
Generally subject to a set of laws called the lands and waters of the United States that
covers what you can do with water in a lot of places in the country.
But Texas property is grandfathered in by the Texas Constitution, even though it hasn't
been its own country for a while.
So you can do things with water in Texas.
You can't really do in the rest of the country.
So in principle, the Landbridge, or Landbridge, could take sourced water from its property
and transport it to New Mexico for use and fracking, and once that water turns into produced
water, it can go right back and be disposed of.
End quote.
Walking away from Eferomo's meeting, my co-host and I have increased respect for the
rising kinetics team and are more bullish on TPL, Landbridge, and Eferomo.
Texas-specific land.
Over the last quarter, TPL announced an acquisition.
Here's the pertinent text from the press release.
TPL acquired mineral interests across approximately 4106 net royalty acres located on Colberton County
Texas.
The acquired mineral interests overlap existing TPL world acreage and current and anticipated
drilling and spacing units, enhancing TPL's net revenue interests in existing and future
wells of oil and gas.
In addition, the acquired mineral interests overlap with TPL surface acreage.
The acquired surface asset spans approximately 4,120 acres in Martin County, Texas, and is
strategically located in the core of the Midland Basin.
The asset generates numerous revenue streams across water supply, produced water disposal,
and multiple other surface-related activities, including royalties from a solids waste
landfill, and possesses significant additional commercial growth opportunities.
End quote.
A chart depicting the acquired rights and acres shown with TPL's legacy acres is displayed
below.
The press release also had the following quote from TPL CEO, quote,
acquiring high-quality mineral interests in the Northern Delaware Basin and strategic
surface acreage in the Midland Basin will immediately contribute to TPL's free cash flow.
The combined asset purchase price implies a greater than 13% 2025 free cash flow yield
at the current strip prices, giving credit to only existing production and line of site
wells and opportunities.
End quote.
If the CEO's estimates prove accurate, then this could prove excellent capital allocation.
Over the long term, we think these estimates will prove conservative.
Conclusion.
With that, we've wrapped up another episode of the show.
Thanks for joining us in our investing journey.
Let us know where we've got something wrong or what we're missing in the comment section.
Thanks for your participation.
We'll see you all in two weeks with another write-up.
